The Solar System: A Brief Reference

The Solar System consists of the Sun and the objects that orbit it, including
eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, and comets.

Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest of the eight planets.
It has no moons and almost no atmosphere. A single orbit around the Sun takes
about 88 Earth days.

Venus is the second planet from the Sun. It is the hottest planet in the Solar
System because of a thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere that traps heat. Surface
temperatures reach roughly 465 degrees Celsius.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only known world to support life.
About 71 percent of Earth's surface is covered by water. Earth has a single
natural satellite, the Moon.

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is often called the Red Planet because
of iron oxide on its surface. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

Jupiter is the fifth planet and by far the largest in the Solar System. It is a
gas giant with a famous storm called the Great Red Spot. Jupiter has dozens of
known moons, the four largest being Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.

Saturn is the sixth planet and is best known for its prominent ring system made
mostly of ice and rock. Saturn is the second-largest planet.

Uranus is the seventh planet and rotates on its side, with an axial tilt of about
98 degrees. It appears blue-green because of methane in its atmosphere.

Neptune is the eighth and farthest known planet from the Sun. It is a cold, windy
ice giant with the strongest sustained winds measured on any planet.
